draft.title: The addition rule
card: Pr(A ∪ B) is the chance that A happens, or B happens, or both. The rule is Pr(A ∪ B) = Pr(A) + Pr(B) − Pr(A ∩ B).
We subtract Pr(A ∩ B) because outcomes in both A and B are counted twice when we add Pr(A) and Pr(B).
Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together, so Pr(A ∩ B) = 0. Then Pr(A ∪ B) = Pr(A) + Pr(B).
Example: Pr(A) = 0.5, Pr(B) = 0.4 and Pr(A ∩ B) = 0.2. Then Pr(A ∪ B) = 0.5 + 0.4 − 0.2 = 0.7.
draft.remember: Add the two chances, then take away the overlap so it is counted once.

a.q: Pr(A) = 0.6, Pr(B) = 0.3 and Pr(A ∩ B) = 0.1. What is Pr(A ∪ B)?
a.why: Pr(A ∪ B) = 0.6 + 0.3 − 0.1 = 0.8. Adding only Pr(A) and Pr(B) gives 0.9, which counts the overlap twice.

b.q: At a Ballarat school, Pr(a student plays netball) = 0.35 and Pr(a student plays chess) = 0.15. No student does both. What is the chance a student plays netball or chess?
b.why: No student does both, so the events are mutually exclusive and Pr(A ∩ B) = 0. Then Pr(A ∪ B) = 0.35 + 0.15 = 0.50. The product 0.0525 is not used here, because the rule adds the chances.
b.clue: If no one does both, what is the overlap?

final.title: The addition rule
card: \(\text{Pr}(A \cup B)\) is the chance that \(A\) happens, or \(B\) happens, or both. The rule is \(\text{Pr}(A \cup B) = \text{Pr}(A) + \text{Pr}(B) - \text{Pr}(A \cap B)\).
We subtract \(\text{Pr}(A \cap B)\) because outcomes in both \(A\) and \(B\) are counted twice when we add \(\text{Pr}(A)\) and \(\text{Pr}(B)\).
Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together, so \(\text{Pr}(A \cap B) = 0\). Then \(\text{Pr}(A \cup B) = \text{Pr}(A) + \text{Pr}(B)\).
final.remember: Add the two chances, then take away the overlap so it is counted once.
